To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the infusion of diversity content into a sequence of undergraduate human development courses resulted in positive changes in attitudes toward low income and ethnic minority groups, as measured by standardized instruments, as well as in the development of critical thinking skills and a more nuanced understanding of poverty as a risk factor.

(1) there is a dearth of empirical studies of the development of low income minority youth; (2) the sampling patterns used in studies on the development of adolescents reinforce a deficit perspective; (3) the infusion of multicultural content into human development courses can decrease ethnocentrism; and (4) the infusion of content can increase students' awareness of poverty as an important developmental risk factor.

(1) the content and research on child and family development is not sufficiently diverse, (2) students in human development courses do not have a sufficient understanding of poverty, and (3) students in human developmental courses can be taught to be more sensitive to poverty and diversity issues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of human diversity in a multicultural world, and how the study of human development can contribute to this process.
the question, how can we best prepare students for the realities of diversity in the lives of children and adolescents?
how the field of human development can become a leader in promoting social justice, by infusing diversity perspectives into our teaching and research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the research on diversity in human development is still in its infancy, and there is an urgent need to infuse diversity into the curriculum.
the evidence is not yet sufficient to warrant a definitive conclusion about the effects of multicultural education on the attitudes of students in human development courses.
the evidence is mixed and the jury is still out on the efficacy of diversity courses in higher education.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are attempting to create a context that will allow students to develop a more critical perspective on the social and cultural construction of knowledge and the role of the social sciences in the perpetuation of social inequalities.
we need more research on the developmental context of minority children and adolescents.

it is possible to infuse a diversity perspective into a human development course without losing the integrity of the discipline.
